name: Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame
description: Master the Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame with expert collar grip mechanics, finishing sequences, and defensive strategies for purple to brown belts.
summary: The Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame is a gi collar choke from modified scarf hold where the opponent's trapped arm clears the defensive frame, letting the attacker set a deep far-side collar grip and shear the forearm blade across both carotid arteries.
overview:
The Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame exploits the unique arm isolation and hip pressure of modified scarf hold to create a high-percentage collar choke. Unlike standard side control breadcutter setups where the opponent can use both arms to strip grips and frame, the trapped arm in Kuzure Kesa-Gatame eliminates the primary defensive barrier. This allows the attacker to feed the far-side collar grip deep across the neck without resistance, transforming a moderate-percentage technique into a reliable finisher.

The mechanics rely on threading the choking hand deep into the far-side collar while positioning the forearm blade directly across the carotid arteries. The attacker uses the existing hip pressure and chest weight from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame to generate choking force through body positioning rather than arm strength alone. The finish comes from sprawling the legs back and expanding the chest, which drives the forearm through the neck in a shearing motion that compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously.

Strategically, this choke functions as the apex of a multi-threat attack chain from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame. When opponents defend americana and kimura threats by keeping their trapped arm bent and tight, the attacker redirects to the collar, attacking the neck rather than the arm. This creates a layered dilemma where arm defense opens neck attacks and vice versa. The breadcutter also punishes opponents who flatten their back to the mat to prevent shoulder locks, as the flat position actually improves the angle for the collar choke. Competition footage consistently shows this finishing opponents who successfully defended arm attacks but failed to address the collar threat.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate with proper release; prolonged compression can cause serious neurological injury

injury_risks.injury: Tracheal damage from misapplied pressure or sudden jerking
injury_risks.recovery_time: 2-6 weeks for minor damage; surgery required for severe cases

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain or cervical spine stress from resisting the choke
Jaw pressure causing temporomandibular joint irritation

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum squeeze in training, never spike or jerk the collar grip
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or any distress vocalization)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body or mat
Any rapid tapping motion with hand or foot
Body going limp (automatic release required immediately)
release_protocol: Immediately release collar grip upon any tap signal
Remove forearm pressure and body weight from opponent's neck
Allow opponent to turn to a safe position and recover breathing
Check that opponent is conscious and breathing normally
Give partner adequate time to recover before continuing training
training_restrictions: Always apply the choke gradually in training, never at competition speed
Never jerk or spike the collar grip into position
Ensure partner has clear access to tap with at least one hand
Stop immediately at any sign of distress even without a tap
Never train this choke on partners with neck, throat, or vascular injuries
Beginners must drill under direct instructor supervision

attacker.name: from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame including collar grip depth, forearm pressure mechanics, and competition finishing sequences.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame leverages the existing arm isolation and hip pressure of modified scarf hold to create a seamless collar choke entry. The position's inherent control means you can hunt the far-side collar without sacrificing positional integrity, since the trapped arm cannot interfere with your grip work. The key is recognizing when your opponent's arm defense opens the collar and committing to the grip depth needed to finish. The choke finishes through body mechanics rather than arm strength, using a sprawl and chest expansion to drive the forearm blade through the carotid arteries.
key_principles: Maintain hip pressure throughout the collar grip hunt to prevent opponent creating escape space
Grip depth determines everything: four fingers deep past the neck midline before committing to the finish
The choking forearm must align with the blade (radius bone) across the carotid arteries, not the flat of the forearm
Finish with body weight and sprawl mechanics, not by squeezing with the arms
Use arm isolation threats to force defensive reactions that open the collar
Keep chest low during the entire sequence to deny framing space to the free arm
setup_requirements: Established Kuzure Kesa-Gatame with secure arm isolation and consistent hip pressure into opponent's ribs
Opponent's trapped arm controlled at both shoulder and wrist, preventing recovery or defensive framing
Access to opponent's far-side collar, which requires managing their free hand's defensive attempts
Low chest position maintained throughout to prevent opponent from creating frames with their free arm
Base leg posted wide enough to maintain stability during the grip transition

execution_steps.action: Maintain position and test collar access
execution_steps.description: From established Kuzure Kesa-Gatame, maintain hip pressure and arm isolation while assessing the far-side collar. Use an americana or kimura feint to draw opponent's free hand into defending the arm, clearing the path to the collar. Do not release hip pressure during this phase.

execution_steps.action: Feed the choking hand into the far-side collar
execution_steps.description: Release your hip-side hand from the near-side grip and thread it palm-up deep into the far-side collar, aiming to get four fingers past the centerline of the opponent's neck. Keep your elbow tight to their chest as you feed the grip to prevent them from framing against your arm.

execution_steps.action: Establish grip depth and forearm alignment
execution_steps.description: Once the collar grip is set, rotate your wrist so the blade of your forearm (radius bone side) presses directly against the side of the opponent's neck over the carotid artery. Pull the collar material tight to eliminate slack, which ensures the forearm maintains direct contact with the neck throughout the finish.

Place your free hand on the mat near the opponent's far hip or grip their near-side collar for additional anchor. This hand provides the base and leverage needed for the finishing sprawl. Avoid grabbing your own wrist, which limits your sprawling range and reduces finishing power.

Drive your legs backward into a sprawl while keeping your hips low. This shifts your body weight forward over the choking arm and increases the downward pressure of the forearm across the neck. Your chest should expand as you sprawl, creating a shearing force that compresses both carotid arteries against the collar material.

execution_steps.action: Drive through the neck to complete the choke
execution_steps.description: Continue the sprawl while pulling the collar grip toward you and expanding your chest outward. The forearm blade drives through the neck in a diagonal cutting motion. Maintain steady progressive pressure until the opponent taps. Never jerk or spike the finish. If the opponent goes limp, release immediately.

execution_steps.action: Manage the finish and release protocol
execution_steps.description: Upon receiving a tap signal, immediately release the collar grip and remove forearm pressure from the neck. Shift your body weight off the opponent and allow them to turn to a safe position. Verify they are conscious and breathing normally before continuing. In competition, maintain control until the referee stops the match.

common_counters.counter: Opponent uses free hand to strip or block the collar grip before it sets deep
common_counters.your_response: Feint the americana or kimura on the trapped arm to draw their free hand into arm defense, then immediately redirect to the collar while their hand is occupied

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you and attempts to recover half guard during the grip transition
common_counters.your_response: Maintain hip pressure and use the collar grip attempt to transition to mount as they turn in, or abandon the choke and consolidate the improved position

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges explosively during the finishing sprawl to create space and escape to guard
common_counters.your_response: Absorb the bridge by widening your base leg and dropping your head past their far shoulder, then re-engage the sprawl once the bridge energy dissipates

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin aggressively to block the forearm from reaching the carotid arteries
common_counters.your_response: The chin tuck is uncomfortable but does not stop a properly set deep collar grip; increase sprawl pressure and the forearm will work past the chin, or use the free hand to redirect the chin

common_errors.error: Insufficient collar grip depth, feeding only two fingers past the neck midline
common_errors.consequence: The forearm cannot reach the carotid arteries and the choke becomes a jaw crush that the opponent can endure without tapping
common_errors.correction: Feed four fingers deep past the centerline of the neck before committing to the finish, pulling slack out of the collar material as you set the grip

common_errors.error: Releasing hip pressure to reach for the collar with both hands
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately creates space and escapes to guard or half guard, losing the entire positional advantage
common_errors.correction: Maintain hip pressure throughout the grip transition by keeping your hips heavy and only releasing one hand at a time to hunt the collar

common_errors.error: Using the flat of the forearm across the neck instead of the blade (radius bone edge)
common_errors.consequence: Pressure disperses across a wide surface area, compressing the trachea rather than targeting the carotid arteries, resulting in an airway choke that is slower and more painful
common_errors.correction: Rotate your wrist to align the radius bone edge against the neck, creating a narrow cutting surface that targets the carotid arteries specifically

common_errors.error: Attempting to finish by squeezing with arm strength rather than sprawling with body weight
common_errors.consequence: Rapid forearm fatigue and insufficient finishing pressure, allowing the opponent time to escape while your grip weakens
common_errors.correction: Drive your legs back in a sprawl and expand your chest to generate choking pressure through body mechanics, keeping the arm as a rigid frame rather than an active squeezer

common_errors.error: Sitting upright during the collar hunt, exposing space under the chest
common_errors.consequence: Opponent's free arm can create effective frames that block the collar grip entry and set up escape sequences
common_errors.correction: Maintain a low chest position throughout, keeping your weight distributed across the opponent's upper body to deny framing space

common_errors.error: Telegraphing the choke by immediately abandoning arm attacks to reach for the collar
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the transition and proactively blocks the collar with their free hand before the grip can be established
common_errors.correction: Use the americana or kimura as a genuine threat first, then redirect to the collar when the opponent commits their free hand to arm defense

training_progressions.focus: Collar grip depth and forearm alignment
training_progressions.description: Partner lies flat with no resistance. Practice feeding the collar grip to four-finger depth, rotating to blade alignment, and removing collar slack. Repeat 20 times each side until the grip sequence is automatic. Focus on hand path and wrist rotation, not finishing pressure.

With collar grip already set, practice the finishing sprawl against a stationary partner. Focus on driving legs back while expanding the chest, generating choking pressure through body positioning. Partner provides feedback on pressure location and intensity. Build to gradual taps.

training_progressions.focus: Chaining from americana and kimura feints to collar entry
training_progressions.description: Partner defends arm attacks at 50% resistance from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame. Practice the full sequence: threaten americana, redirect to collar when free hand defends arm, set grip, and finish. Increase partner resistance by 10% each round. Focus on smooth transitions that maintain hip pressure.

Start from established Kuzure Kesa-Gatame with partner at 70-100% resistance. Apply the full attack chain including arm threats and collar choke. Partner works genuine escapes and defenses. Track success rate across rounds and identify grip timing adjustments needed against active resistance.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Breadcutter Choke primarily attack and how does the forearm position target them?
flashcards.answer: The Breadcutter Choke primarily attacks both carotid arteries by positioning the blade (radius bone edge) of the forearm diagonally across the lateral neck. The collar material behind the neck acts as a fulcrum while the forearm drives into the carotid arteries from the front. This bilateral compression restricts blood flow to the brain, producing unconsciousness within seconds when properly applied.

trap: Crank the neck spine to finish

flashcards.question: What physical indicators tell you the choke is properly set and approaching the finish?
flashcards.answer: The opponent's face begins to change color, typically reddening from venous congestion. Their defensive movements become less coordinated and more panicked. You feel a distinct decrease in resistance through the collar grip as their neck muscles fatigue. The forearm feels firmly seated against yielding tissue rather than bone, indicating proper carotid targeting rather than tracheal compression. The opponent may begin making involuntary sounds.

flashcards.question: What control must be established before you begin hunting the far-side collar grip?
flashcards.answer: You must have secure Kuzure Kesa-Gatame with consistent hip pressure into the opponent's ribs, the trapped arm controlled at both shoulder and wrist preventing recovery, a low chest position denying frames, and your base leg posted wide for stability. Without these four elements, reaching for the collar creates space that the opponent will exploit to escape before the choke can be established.
flashcards.answer_line: Pin hips, control arm, chest low

plausible: Just trap the far arm tightly
Post both knees and sit up tall

flashcards.question: At what point during the setup does the Breadcutter Choke become nearly impossible to defend?
flashcards.answer: Once the collar grip is set with four fingers past the neck midline and the forearm blade is rotated into contact with the carotid arteries, the choke is extremely difficult to defend. The opponent cannot strip a deep collar grip with one free hand while their other arm is trapped, and the sprawling finish generates force through body weight that no amount of neck muscular resistance can overcome. The critical defensive window closes when the grip passes the midline.

plausible: Once any collar grip is set
trap: Wait for the sprawl, then defend

flashcards.question: What is the most common reason the Breadcutter Choke fails to produce a tap from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame?
flashcards.answer: Insufficient collar grip depth is the most common failure. When only two or three fingers pass the neck midline, the forearm cannot reach the carotid arteries and instead presses against the jaw or trachea. This produces pain but not the rapid blood flow restriction needed for the choke. The opponent can endure jaw pressure and work escapes during the extended application time. Always prioritize grip depth over speed of the finish.

trap: Lift your chest to crank harder

flashcards.question: How should you adjust your grip and pressure angle if the opponent tucks their chin aggressively?
flashcards.answer: A properly deep collar grip renders chin tucking ineffective because the forearm is already past the chin line when the grip is set at four-finger depth. If the chin blocks your forearm, your grip is too shallow and needs to be reset deeper. You can also use your free hand to redirect the chin upward momentarily while driving the choking forearm into position. Never try to force the forearm past the chin with strength alone, as this creates tracheal pressure instead of a clean blood choke.

plausible: Wait for them to tire out

flashcards.question: What are the critical safety protocols when training the Breadcutter Choke?
flashcards.answer: Always apply the choke gradually over 3-5 seconds minimum in training, never jerking or spiking the collar grip. Ensure your partner has at least one hand free to tap at all times. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal, physical hand tap, foot tap, or body going limp. After release, remove all weight from the neck area and verify your partner is conscious and breathing normally. Never train this on partners with existing neck or vascular conditions.
flashcards.answer_line: Apply slowly, release on any tap

plausible: Trap both arms for a clean rep
Set the grip fast, finish slow
trap: Hold choke after tap to confirm

flashcards.question: How should you release the Breadcutter Choke after your training partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Upon any tap signal, immediately open your collar grip and remove the forearm from the neck. Shift your body weight off the opponent's upper body and allow them space to turn to a safe position. Check that they are alert, conscious, and breathing normally. If they appear dazed or do not respond quickly, place them in a recovery position and seek medical attention. Never maintain any neck pressure after a tap, even to maintain the position for a reset.

plausible: Stand up and reset for next round
trap: Keep weight on neck till they move

flashcards.question: How does the Breadcutter Choke integrate with americana and kimura threats from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame to create a submission chain?
flashcards.answer: The arm isolation in Kuzure Kesa-Gatame creates a natural dilemma: the opponent must use their free hand to either defend their trapped arm from americana and kimura attacks or protect their collar from the breadcutter. Threatening the americana first forces the free hand to defend the arm, clearing a path to the collar. If they leave the arm to protect the collar, finish the americana. This creates a lose-lose scenario where defending one attack opens the other.
flashcards.answer_line: Threaten arm lock, free the collar

trap: Release arm control for the collar

flashcards.question: How does the finishing strategy differ when applying this choke in competition versus training?
flashcards.answer: In competition, you apply the choke with full body commitment and faster sprawl mechanics once the grip is set deep, since the opponent is fighting at maximum resistance and may attempt to endure discomfort. Maintain the choke until the referee intervenes. In training, apply slowly and progressively over several seconds, giving your partner ample opportunity to tap. Never use competition intensity in training. The grip setup should be identical in both contexts, but the finishing pressure ramp differs significantly.

trap: Spike the choke fast in training

defender.name: from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame Defender
defender.description: Defend against the Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame with early recognition cues, collar grip prevention methods, and systematic escape sequences.
defender.overview: Defending the Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame demands early recognition and proactive grip prevention, because once the collar grip is set deep past the neck midline, defensive options become severely limited. The trapped arm in Kuzure Kesa-Gatame means you have only one free hand to address both the collar threat and positional escapes, making timing and priority management critical. Successful defense requires understanding the attacker's grip progression and intercepting it before the forearm reaches the carotid arteries, while simultaneously working to recover the trapped arm or escape the position entirely.
key_principles: The defensive window is narrowest after the collar grip sets deep: prioritize preventing the grip over countering the finish
Your free hand must address the collar threat first, arm recovery second, since the choke is immediately dangerous while the pin is survivable
Track the attacker's hip-side hand at all times, as its release from near-side control signals the collar hunt is beginning
Bridge timing must coincide with the attacker's weight transition during the grip change, not during established heavy pressure
Turning toward the attacker paradoxically reduces choke effectiveness by changing the angle of the forearm across the neck
Tap early in training when the grip is set and the sprawl begins rather than trying to endure arterial compression
recognition_cues: The attacker releases their near-side hand control (the hand closest to your hips) to reach across toward your far collar
You feel a reduction in arm isolation pressure as the attacker redirects one hand from controlling your trapped arm to hunting the collar
The attacker's weight shifts forward and toward your head as they thread the choking hand into the collar
You feel fabric tightening against the back of your neck as the collar grip is being set and slack removed

defensive_options.action: Block the collar grip with your free hand by posting it against the attacker's bicep or wrist before the grip sets
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the attacker release their near-side hand and begin reaching across toward your far collar
defensive_options.if_successful: The choke attempt is neutralized and the attacker must return to positional control, buying time for escape attempts
defensive_options.risk: Committing your free hand to grip defense leaves no frame available for escape and may open arm attack opportunities

defensive_options.action: Bridge explosively toward the attacker's posting leg during the collar grip transition when their weight is shifting
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the 1-2 second window when the attacker is transitioning from arm control to collar grip and their weight distribution is compromised
defensive_options.if_successful: The attacker is forced to abandon the collar hunt to re-establish base, resetting the position and buying time
defensive_options.risk: If mistimed against peak pressure, the bridge wastes energy without creating positional change

defensive_options.action: Turn into the attacker and recover closed guard by threading your near-side knee across their belly during the grip transition
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits both hands away from hip control to pursue the collar grip, creating space for hip movement
defensive_options.if_successful: You escape to closed guard, neutralizing both the choke and the positional disadvantage entirely
defensive_options.risk: If the collar grip is already deep, turning into the attacker may accelerate the choke finish rather than facilitate escape

escape_paths: Block the collar grip early with your free hand, then use the positional reset to work standard Kuzure Kesa-Gatame escapes such as the bridge and roll or elbow escape
Time an explosive bridge to coincide with the attacker releasing near-side control, then hip escape away to recover half guard or full guard
Turn into the attacker during the grip transition and thread your knee across their belly to recover closed guard before the choke sets

favorable_outcomes.how: Exploit the attacker's reduced hip control during the collar grip transition by turning into them and threading your knee across to recover closed guard

common_errors.error: Attempting to strip the collar grip after it has been set deep past the neck midline
common_errors.consequence: The grip is mechanically locked by the collar material and body weight, making it nearly impossible to strip with one hand, while the time spent trying allows the attacker to begin the finishing sprawl
common_errors.correction: Intercept the collar grip during the feeding phase before it passes the midline, when the hand is still threading through the collar and vulnerable to blocking

common_errors.error: Using the free hand to push the attacker's chest instead of addressing the collar grip
common_errors.consequence: The push has no meaningful effect on an attacker with a low chest position and strong base, while the collar grip sets uncontested and the choke finishes
common_errors.correction: Direct the free hand to the attacker's wrist or bicep to block the collar entry, addressing the immediate choking threat rather than trying to create general space

common_errors.error: Panicking and bridging straight up when the forearm contacts the neck
common_errors.consequence: An upward bridge against a sprawled attacker creates no positional change and wastes explosive energy that could be used for a properly angled escape
common_errors.correction: Bridge at an angle toward the attacker's posting leg to attack their base structure, or turn into the attacker to change the forearm angle across the neck

common_errors.error: Ignoring the collar threat to focus entirely on recovering the trapped arm
common_errors.consequence: The collar grip sets uncontested while you work arm recovery, and the choke finishes before the arm can be recovered
common_errors.correction: Prioritize the collar threat when you detect the attacker hunting the grip, since the choke is immediately dangerous while the arm pin is survivable

flashcards.question: How do you recognize the Breadcutter Choke is being set up from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame?
flashcards.answer: The primary recognition cue is the attacker releasing their near-side hand from controlling your trapped arm or hips. You will feel a reduction in arm isolation pressure followed by fabric movement at your collar as their hand threads across. Their weight shifts forward toward your head. The moment you feel the collar tightening against the back of your neck, the grip is being set and you must act immediately.

plausible: Their base leg steps over you
trap: Ignore it, arm control still there

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Breadcutter Choke to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap as soon as you feel the forearm blade set against your neck and the attacker begin their sprawl. Do not attempt to endure the choke once the grip is deep and the finishing pressure has begun, as unconsciousness from bilateral carotid compression occurs within seconds and without warning. In training, tap early to signal your partner before full pressure is applied. Use verbal, hand, or foot taps, whichever is accessible.

plausible: Turn to your side first, then tap
Tap only if you cannot bridge out
trap: Try to endure and fight through it

flashcards.question: What is the most effective time window to defend the Breadcutter Choke from this position?
flashcards.answer: The optimal defensive window is the 1-2 seconds during which the attacker releases their near-side hand to reach for the collar. During this transition, their arm control and hip pressure are momentarily reduced, creating opportunity to block the collar grip, bridge against their compromised base, or turn into them to recover guard. Once the grip passes the neck midline, defensive options are extremely limited.

trap: Wait for the sprawl to defend

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the Breadcutter Choke from Kuzure Kesa-Gatame?
flashcards.answer: The three primary defenses are: (1) blocking the collar grip with your free hand before it sets deep, targeting the attacker's wrist or bicep during the feeding phase; (2) bridging explosively toward the attacker's posting leg during the grip transition when their weight is shifting; and (3) turning into the attacker to recover closed guard while their hip control is reduced. All three are most effective during the grip transition window.
flashcards.answer_line: Block grip, bridge, turn to guard

plausible: Strip grip after it's set deep
Pull head down and turtle up
trap: Push away and expose your back

flashcards.question: Why is turning toward the attacker sometimes more effective than turning away when defending this choke?
flashcards.answer: Turning toward the attacker changes the angle at which the forearm contacts your neck, potentially shifting it from the carotid arteries to a less effective position across the jaw or chin. It also closes the distance between your bodies, reducing the sprawling range the attacker needs to generate finishing pressure. Additionally, turning in creates the opportunity to thread your knee across and recover guard, addressing both the choke and the positional disadvantage simultaneously.

plausible: Removes all of their hip pressure
Lets you post on the free arm
trap: Turn away and give up the back

training_progressions.description: Partner establishes Kuzure Kesa-Gatame and alternates between maintaining the pin and hunting the collar. Practice identifying the exact moment the collar hunt begins based on hand release and weight shift cues. No escape attempts yet, just recognition. Build a reliable early warning system before adding defensive responses.

training_progressions.focus: Blocking the collar grip during the feeding phase
training_progressions.description: Partner reaches for the collar at 50% speed. Practice intercepting with your free hand at the wrist or bicep before the grip passes the neck midline. Increase partner speed progressively. Focus on hand placement accuracy and timing rather than strength. Track success rate to measure improvement.

training_progressions.focus: Combining grip prevention with positional escapes
training_progressions.description: Partner works the full attack sequence at 70% intensity. Practice chaining grip prevention into bridges, guard recovery, and standard Kuzure Kesa-Gatame escapes. Build the habit of using the attacker's grip transition as an escape opportunity rather than a purely defensive moment.

training_progressions.focus: Full-speed defense against committed choke attempts
training_progressions.description: Start from established Kuzure Kesa-Gatame with partner at full resistance. Defend the breadcutter while also managing other submission threats. Practice decision-making about when to prioritize collar defense versus positional escape. Tap early when caught to build safe training habits.
